slides.title: Total protein
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Often included in a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) and used to help diagnose kidney disease, liver disease or nutritional problems. Also ordered to check or monitor conditions affecting protein levels, or with symptoms such as swelling from fluid in tissues, fatigue, unexplained weight loss, jaundice or blood in the urine.

Physiology: The test measures the total amount of protein in the blood, made up of two major types: albumin, which forms most of it, and globulins. It also compares the two as the albumin/globulin (A/G) ratio.

slides.title: Total protein
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Albumin is made in the liver; it helps keep fluid inside blood vessels and carries hormones, medicines and vitamins. Globulins help fight infection and move nutrients; some are made by the liver and others by the immune system.

slides.title: Total protein
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
cols: Possible causes of high total protein: an infection such as HIV or viral hepatitis, and multiple myeloma (a type of blood cancer).
A high A/G ratio may be caused by certain types of genetic disorders or leukemia.
Possible causes of low total protein: liver disease, kidney disease, malnutrition and malabsorption syndromes (such as celiac disease and Crohn's disease).
A low A/G ratio may be caused by an autoimmune disease such as lupus, liver disease including cirrhosis, or kidney disease.

slides.title: Total protein
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: Tell the provider about all medicines taken; stop any only if the provider says so. If the test is part of another blood test, fasting for several hours may be needed.

Limitations: The result is interpreted together with symptoms, medical history and other blood tests. A separate albumin test and/or serum electrophoresis, which measures four types of globulins, may also be ordered.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (serum)

What it is used for: Used to check general health and nutrition and how well the liver and kidneys work, and to monitor treatment of conditions that affect albumin. A damaged liver or poor nutrition can reduce albumin production, and damaged kidneys may let albumin pass into the urine. Often part of a liver panel or comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP).

Physiology: Albumin is a protein made by the liver. It keeps the fluid part of the blood from leaking out of blood vessels into tissues and carries hormones, vitamins and enzymes; with too little albumin, fluid can build up in the lungs, abdomen or elsewhere.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: High albumin may be a sign of dehydration, which can be caused by severe diarrhea or other conditions.

Low: Possible causes of low albumin: liver disease (including severe cirrhosis, hepatitis and steatotic liver disease), kidney disease, malnutrition (especially lack of protein in the diet), infection, digestive diseases that impair use of protein from food (such as Crohn's disease and malabsorption disorders), burns over a large area of the body and thyroid disease.

slides.title: Albumin
slides.eyebrow: Proteins and inflammation · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for albumin itself; fasting for several hours may be needed if other blood tests are ordered. Some medicines can affect the result, so tell the provider what is being taken.

Interferences: An out-of-range result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Steroids, insulin and hormones can raise albumin; not eating for 24–48 hours and some medicines, including birth control pills, can lower it, and albumin is lower during pregnancy.
Limitations: An albumin test alone cannot diagnose a condition; the provider usually interprets it together with other test results.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
rows: clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) + CRAB or SLiM (≥60% plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm on MRI) %

slides.title: A patient with low albumin has swelling of the legs and abdomen. Which function of albumin explains this?
options: Albumin breaks down old red blood cells as they circulate in the blood
Albumin is the main blood-clotting protein, so when it is low, fluid and blood seep out of the vessels
Albumin keeps fluid inside blood vessels; when it is low, fluid can leak into tissues and build up
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source says that without enough albumin, fluid can build up in the lungs, abdomen or other parts of the body.

Basis: MedlinePlus: albumin keeps the fluid part of the blood from leaking out of blood vessels; without enough albumin, fluid can build up in various parts of the body.

slides.title: Which possible explanation for a high albumin level does the source give?
options: Dehydration, for example from severe diarrhea
Kidney damage letting albumin pass into the urine
Malnutrition
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source says high albumin may be a sign of dehydration; steroids, insulin and hormones can also raise it.

Basis: MedlinePlus: higher than normal albumin may be a sign of dehydration, which may be caused by severe diarrhea or other conditions.

slides.title: Why is the A/G ratio reported together with total protein?
options: The A/G ratio measures how fast the liver clears bilirubin
Total protein is made up of albumin and globulins; comparing them adds information — for example, a low ratio may occur with autoimmune, liver or kidney disease
The A/G ratio makes all other tests unnecessary
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: the source lists separate possible causes for a low and a high A/G ratio.

Basis: MedlinePlus: blood has two major types of protein, albumin and globulin; the test compares them as the A/G ratio, and a low ratio may be caused by autoimmune, liver or kidney disease.

slides.title: Total protein is high. Which possible cause does the source list?
options: Malnutrition, with too little protein taken in from food
Celiac disease, which impairs the absorption of nutrients from the gut
Multiple myeloma, or an infection such as HIV or viral hepatitis
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: these are the possible causes of high total protein given by the source.

Basis: MedlinePlus: high total protein may be a sign of an infection such as HIV or viral hepatitis, or of multiple myeloma.

slides.title: Which tests are important for diagnosing multiple myeloma:
options: Determining ESR
Determining total protein in blood serum and pathological immunoglobulins
Determining Bence Jones protein in urine, increase of plasma cells in the myelogram
All tests are important

slides.title: Plasma cells are formed:
options: from macrophages
from B lymphocytes
from fibroblasts
from lymphocytes

slides.title: A high percentage of plasma cells in bone marrow is observed:
options: In collagen diseases
In infectious mononucleosis

slides.title: Multiple myeloma. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
bullets: 1. Multiple myeloma is a tumor of clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow; a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) or free light chains are produced.

2. Diagnosis (IMWG): clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) + a myeloma-defining event: CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia, lytic bone lesions) or SLiM biomarkers (plasma cells ≥60%, involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion ≥5 mm on MRI).

slides.title: Multiple myeloma. Clinical and laboratory parameters?
bullets: 3. Laboratory: protein electrophoresis (M-spike) and immunofixation (serum and urine), free light chains (kappa/lambda ratio), total protein, albumin, calcium, creatinine.
4. Blood: normocytic anemia, erythrocytes in "stacks of coins" (rouleaux) on the smear, ESR markedly raised; rarely circulating plasma cells.
5. Urine: Bence Jones protein (light chains) – a test strip detects it poorly, electrophoresis/immunofixation is needed.
6. Bone marrow: number and clonality of plasma cells (immunophenotype), cytogenetics/FISH – prognosis.
